title: Atrioventricular Septal Defect
subject: Paediatrics
summary: A congenital heart lesion where the atrioventricular septum is deficient, causing a common AV valve and left‑to‑right shunting. It presents with failure to thrive, tachypnoea and a systolic ejection murmur. Early diagnosis and surgical repair optimise outcomes.

sections.p: AVSD is a failure of the endocardial cushions to fuse, producing a single AV valve and a defect in the atrial and ventricular septa. Diagnosis is clinical plus imaging.
b: Systolic ejection murmur, often harsh, best heard at left upper sternal border
Digital clubbing may appear late
Failure to thrive, tachypnoea, easy cyanosis

t.b: Shows cardiomegaly and increased pulmonary vascular markings – indicates volume overload
Gold standard; confirms single AV valve, size of shunt, pulmonary pressures and ventricular function
Detects hypoxaemia; SpO2 <92% on room air suggests significant shunt

sections.p: Severity is graded by the magnitude of left‑to‑right shunt and pulmonary hypertension. The Ross classification (I–IV) is commonly used.
b: Stage I – small shunt, normal pulmonary pressures
Stage II – moderate shunt, mild pulmonary hypertension
Stage III – large shunt, moderate pulmonary hypertension
Stage IV – large shunt, severe pulmonary hypertension and right‑ventricular failure

sections.p: The primary cause is genetic, most often trisomy 21. Other associations include Turner syndrome, 22q11.2 deletion and maternal diabetes.
b: Trisomy 21 – accounts for ~90% of cases
Turner syndrome – 5–10%
Maternal diabetes – 2–5%

t.b: Detects AVSD antenatally; allows early referral

sections.p: Infants present with tachypnoea, poor feeding, failure to thrive and a harsh systolic murmur. Older children may have exercise intolerance and cyanosis.
b: Tachypnoea >40 breaths/min in infants
Poor feeding, weight <5th percentile
Harsh systolic ejection murmur at left upper sternal border

t.b: Assess for clubbing, hepatomegaly, and signs of pulmonary hypertension

sections.p: Investigation strategy prioritises bedside echocardiography and basic labs, with escalation if resources allow.
b: Echocardiography – mandatory
Chest X‑ray – supportive

t.b: May show right‑axis deviation and right‑ventricular hypertrophy – indicates volume overload
Anemia may worsen symptoms; look for hemoglobin <10 g/dL
Rule out infective endocarditis if fever present

sections.p: Urgent red flags include severe cyanosis, pulmonary oedema, and shock. Long‑term complications are pulmonary hypertension and arrhythmias.
b: Severe cyanosis (SpO2 <85%)
Pulmonary oedema – crackles, tachypnoea
Shock – hypotension, altered mental status

t.b: Detects hypoxaemia and acidosis – indicates respiratory compromise

sections.p: Management is staged: initial supportive care, then definitive surgical repair. Medical therapy targets volume overload and infection prevention.
b: Diuretics – relieve pulmonary congestion
Beta‑blockers – reduce heart rate and afterload
Prophylactic antibiotics – for dental procedures

t.b: Timing depends on severity; early repair (<1 year) improves survival
Monitor for residual shunt, arrhythmias, and pulmonary hypertension

sections.p: Regular follow‑up with echocardiography and growth monitoring is essential. Prevention focuses on maternal health and early detection of Down syndrome.
b: Annual echocardiography until adulthood
Growth charts – weight and height percentiles

t.b: Ensure pneumococcal and influenza vaccines to prevent respiratory infections

sections.p: AVSD can be mistaken for isolated ASD, VSD or tetralogy of Fallot.
b: Isolated ASD – separate AV valves, no common valve
VSD – separate AV valves, no common valve
Tetralogy of Fallot – cyanosis, harsh systolic murmur but different anatomy

sections.p: Low‑resource settings may misinterpret a normal chest X‑ray as normal if cardiomegaly is subtle.
b: Chest X‑ray – cardiomegaly may be mild early on
Echocardiography – may be unavailable; rely on clinical signs

t.b: May be normal if shunt is small; repeat after feeding or exertion

whenToSeekHelp: Severe cyanosis (SpO2 <85%), pulmonary oedema, shock, sudden worsening of symptoms

faq.q: Why is Down syndrome so closely linked to AVSD?
faq.a: Trisomy 21 disrupts endocardial cushion development, leading to a common AV valve and septal defects.
Yes, detailed fetal echo after 20 weeks can detect a common AV valve and shunt.

faq.q: What is the first step if echocardiography is not available?
faq.a: Use bedside auscultation, pulse oximetry and chest X‑ray to suspect AVSD and refer urgently for echo.

exam: What clinical sign would prompt you to suspect AVSD in a 3‑month‑old? — Harsh systolic ejection murmur at left upper sternal border, tachypnoea and poor feeding.
How would you differentiate AVSD from isolated VSD on exam? — AVSD has a single AV valve and a harsh murmur; VSD has a harsh murmur but separate AV valves.
What is the most appropriate first‑line medical therapy for a child with AVSD and pulmonary oedema? — Diuretics to reduce pulmonary congestion.
When is surgical repair indicated for AVSD? — When pulmonary pressures are <2/3 systemic or when the child shows failure to thrive or progressive symptoms.
Why is prophylactic antibiotic therapy recommended for dental procedures in AVSD patients? — To prevent infective endocarditis in a high‑risk heart lesion.
What red flag would require immediate transfer to a tertiary centre? — Severe cyanosis with SpO2 <85% or signs of shock.
